title: Exploration: the banked set plus the witness-only classification lemma, the lifting step without unused counts, and one first-mark lemma

add.label: Lemma 4.5'
add.name: Rank bound, inequality only
add.proof:
(a) Let $M$ be the matrix of all rows of all $W_c$, of rank $d := \operatorname{rank} \mathbf{W}$, and fix $u$. Choose $d$ linearly independent columns of $M$, column $0$ among them unless it is zero. Given the entries of $r$ at the other indices in $[N]$, at most one value modulo $q$ of its entries at the chosen indices solves $M r = u$. Each of the independent entries $r_1, \dots, r_N$ takes a given value modulo $q$ with probability at most $1/g$, as $g + 1 < q$; so does $r_0$ given all of them. Hence $\Pr[M r = u] \le g^{-d}$, as in Odlyzko's lemma \cite[Lemma 3.1]{NW22}.
(b) Write $v = \sum_c W_c^\top z_c$. Then $v^\top r = \sum_c z_c^\top W_c r$ is a function of $(W_c r)_c$, so it takes one value whenever $(W_c r)_c$ takes its likeliest value, and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top) \ge \operatorname{gp}(\mathbf{W})$.
add.explain: A stack of rank d is guessed with probability at most g^(-d), and a vector of its row space is at least as easy to guess as the stack.

add.label: Lemma B.2'
add.name: Generic bound
add.statement: $E$ is a polynomial of degree two in $u$ with nonnegative coefficients. If $E(2) \le 2^{-\lambda}$ and $E(2^{\lambda+1}) - E(2) \le 1 - 2^{-\lambda}$, then $E(2Q + 2) \le (Q+1)/2^\lambda$ for every integer $0 \le Q < 2^\lambda$.
add.proof: Every term of $E(u)$ is a polynomial in $u$ with nonnegative coefficients, as $L \ge 1$, of degree two for $N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u)$ and at most two otherwise. So $Q \mapsto E(2Q+2) - (Q+1)/2^\lambda$ is convex; by the premises it is at most $0$ at $Q = 0$ and at $Q = 2^\lambda - 1$, where it is $E(2^{\lambda+1}) - 1$, hence in between.
add.explain: The budget E(u) is a quadratic in u with nonnegative coefficients. If E(2) ≤ 2^(−λ) and E(2^(λ+1)) − E(2) ≤ 1 − 2^(−λ), then E(2Q+2) ≤ (Q+1)/2^λ for every Q < 2^λ. Proof idea: Convexity: the difference is at most zero at both ends of the range, hence in between. Note: E has pieces that no lemma of the paper draws on, among them the “+L” of its first term, most of its fifth term, and its sixth term. The paper says its bounds fit “with terms of E(u) to spare”, because E is the bound of the Lean statement.

add.label: Lemma 5.5'
add.name: Search range
add.statement: Let $w \in \{0,1\}^{N+1}$ with $w_0 = 1$, and let $r \leftarrow \mathcal{D}_g$ and $c_w$ be the center of Section 5.2. Then $|r(w) - c_w| \le B$ for every $r$ in the support, and the expectation of $(r(w) - c_w)^2$ is at most $\bigl( g \sqrt{(N+4)/48} + 3/2 \bigr)^2$.
add.proof: Let $a := \lceil N(g+1)/2 \rceil$, $\Sigma := \sum_{i \in [N]} r_i$, and $X := r_\star + \sum_{i \in [N]} (w_i - 1/2)\, r_i$, a sum of $N + 1$ independent terms. Each of $r_\star, r_1, \dots, r_N$ has mean $(g+3)/2$, lies within $(g-1)/2$ of it, and has variance $(g^2-1)/12$. So, as $|w_i - 1/2| = 1/2$, $X$ has mean $\mu := \frac{g+3}{2} (1 + \operatorname{wt}(w) - N/2)$ and variance $(N+4)(g^2-1)/48$, and $|X - \mu| \le (N+2)(g-1)/4$. As $w_0 = 1$, $r(w) = r_0 + \sum_{i \in [N]} w_i r_i = a + X + \Sigma/2 - \lfloor \Sigma/2 \rfloor$, and $c_w = \lfloor a + \mu \rfloor$, so $r(w) - c_w = (X - \mu) + \theta$ for the sum $\theta \in [0, 3/2)$ of the rounding errors $\Sigma/2 - \lfloor \Sigma/2 \rfloor \le 1/2$ and $a + \mu - \lfloor a + \mu \rfloor < 1$. So $|r(w) - c_w| \le (N+2)(g-1)/4 + 3/2 \le (N+1)(g-1)/2 + (N+1)(g+3)/2 = B$, and by Minkowski's inequality in $L^2$ the square root of the expectation of $(r(w) - c_w)^2$ is at most $\sqrt{(N+4)(g^2-1)/48} + 3/2 \le g \sqrt{(N+4)/48} + 3/2$.
add.explain: |r(w) − c_w| ≤ B for every r in the support of the sampler, and E[(r(w) − c_w)²] ≤ (g·√((N+4)/48) + 3/2)² for the centered sampler. Proof idea: r(w) − c_w is a sum of independent centered terms plus two rounding errors.

add.label: Lemma B.8'
add.name: Packing a short multiple
add.statement: Let the parameters satisfy (P3). If $x$ is a short multiple of a kernel vector, then $\hat x \in R^\ell$, with the $\hat x_j$ of Definition 5.1 over $\mathbb{Z}$, solves MSIS for the matrix $A$ of the columns $1, \dots, \ell$ of $M$ (Definition 3.3): $0 < \|\hat x\|_\infty \le \beta$ and $A \hat x = 0 \bmod q$.
add.proof: Modulo $q$, $x$ is a nonzero multiple of a kernel vector $v$; as $z$ is linear and $z(v) = 0$, $x \not\equiv 0$ and $\varphi_e(x) \equiv 0 \bmod q$ for every $e$. As $\varphi_0(x) = x_0$ and $|x_0| \le \beta < q$ by (P3), $x_0 = 0$. So the columns $1, \dots, \ell$ of $M$ map $\hat x$ to zero modulo $q$: the criterion of Definition 5.1 for a vector with entry $0$ zero in the kernel of every form. The coefficients of $\hat x$ are $x_1, \dots, x_N$ and zeros, so $\|\hat x\|_\infty = \|x\|_\infty \le \beta$, and positive, as $x \not\equiv 0$ and $x_0 = 0$.
add.explain: Clause (c) of the heavy stacks lemma, alone: a short multiple of a kernel vector is an MSIS solution.

add.label: Lemma B.7'
add.name: Inverse theorem
add.statement: Let $q$ be prime, and let $N$, $g$, $\theta$, and the integer $\beta$ satisfy the conditions (I1) to (I6) of the inverse theorem, for an integer $b$ and positive reals $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $R_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $\Lambda_1, \Lambda_2, \Lambda_3$, $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2, \Gamma_3$, $A_{\mathrm{inv}}$, $P_1$, and $P_2$. Then every nonzero $v \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ with $v_0 = 0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top) > \theta$ has a short multiple $x$, and $x_0 = 0$.
add.proof:
For $i = 1, \dots, N_0$ in turn, we find a regular saturated lattice $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^{[i]}$ of a rank $d \in [3]$ with $v_{[i]} \in \bar\Theta$ and $m(\Theta) \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i]}^\top) - 3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$; so $m(\Theta) > \theta - 3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} > \mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, as $\theta < \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i]}^\top) \le 1/g$ for $i \in [N_0]$, and $h(\Theta) \le H_d$, for $d \le 2$ by regularity, as $H_d = \Gamma_d/(g^d \mu_{\mathrm{tr}})$, and for $d = 3$ by Lemma B.18(c). For $i = 1$, $\mathbb{Z}^{[1]}$ serves: its reduction $\mathbb{F}_q$ contains $v_{[1]}$, its fibers are points, so $m = 1/g \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[1]}^\top)$, and $h = 1 \le \Gamma_1$, by (I4) and $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}} < 1/g$.

\emph{Adding a coordinate.} Let $i < N_0$, and let $\Theta$ have a largest minor at $J$. Restriction to $J$ maps $\Theta$ injectively (Lemma B.17(a)) onto a lattice of determinant $h(\Theta)$ in $\mathbb{R}^J$. As the unit ball of $\|\cdot\|_1$ has volume $2^d/d!$, the successive minima $\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_d$ of that lattice for $\|\cdot\|_1$ have $\lambda_1 \cdots \lambda_d \le d!\, h(\Theta)$, by Minkowski's second theorem \cite[Chapter VIII, Theorem V]{Cas97}; and by Mahler's lemma \cite[Chapter V, Lemma 8]{Cas97}, for linearly independent vectors that attain them, the lattice has a basis of $\ell_1$ norms at most $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$, and $\max\{\lambda_3, (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3)/2\} \le \frac32 \lambda_3$. So, by the same part, $\Theta$ has a basis matrix $B$ with $\prod_j \|B e_j\|_\infty \le h(\Theta)$, $2h(\Theta)$, or $9h(\Theta)$ for $d = 1, 2, 3$.

As $v_{[i]} \in \bar\Theta$, $v_{[i]} = B c' \bmod q$ for some $c' \in \mathbb{F}_q^d$; with $c := (c', v_{i+1})$ and $\Phi(r) := (B^\top r_{[i]}, r_{i+1})$, $v_{[i+1]}^\top r = c^\top \Phi(r) \bmod q$. Let $F$ be a densest modular fiber $\{ r : v_{[i+1]}^\top r = t \bmod q \}$ of $v_{[i+1]}$, trimmed by $\Theta$, so that $\Pr[F] \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top) - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} > \theta - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by Lemma B.19 and $\operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top) > \theta$. As $v_{i+1} \ne 0$, $\Phi(F)$ lies in a coset of the subgroup $\{ y \in \mathbb{Z}^{d+1} : c^\top y = 0 \bmod q \}$ of index $q$, so $k := \dim \Phi(F) \le d$: otherwise Lemma B.20(a), regularity, and (I5) would give $\Pr[F] \le \Lambda_d \Gamma_d/q < \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} < \theta - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.

Let $\Delta$ be the matrix of the differences of the points of $\Phi(F)$, of rank $k$. By the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality $(e_j^\top y)^2 \le (e_j^\top \Sigma_\Theta e_j)(y^\top \Sigma_\Theta^{-1} y)$, with $e_j^\top \Sigma_\Theta e_j \le \frac{g^2 N}{12} \|B e_j\|_\infty^2$, entries $j$ of two points of $\mathcal{T}_\Theta$ differ by at most $2 R_{\mathrm{tr}}\, g \sqrt{N/12}\, \|B e_j\|_\infty = T_{\mathrm{tr}} \|B e_j\|_\infty$, which bounds the entries of the row $j \in [d]$ of $\Delta$; those of its last row are at most $g - 1 < T_{\mathrm{tr}}$, as $R_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge 20$. As $T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and the $\|B e_j\|_\infty$ are at least $1$, the $k \times k$ minors of $\Delta$, at most $k!$ times a product of $k$ of these bounds, are at most $d!\, T_{\mathrm{tr}}^d \prod_j \|B e_j\|_\infty$, which is at most $H_1 T_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $4 H_2 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^2$, or $54 H_3 T_{\mathrm{tr}}^3$, below $q$ by (I5). As $c^\top \Delta = 0 \bmod q$, Lemma B.17(c), for an integer vector that reduces to $c$, gives $c = u \bmod q$ for a $u \in \mathbb{Z}^{d+1}$ with $u^\top \Delta = 0$. Then $(B u_{[d]}, u_{d+1})^\top r = u^\top \Phi(r)$ is constant on $F$, so $(B u_{[d]}, u_{d+1}) \in F^\perp$, and it reduces to $(B c', v_{i+1}) = v_{[i+1]}$; so $v_{[i+1]} \in \overline{F^\perp}$ and $F^\perp \ne \{0\}$. Then $m(F^\perp) \ge \Pr[F] > \theta - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge \mu_{\mathrm{tr}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, so $F^\perp$ has rank in $[3]$, by (I5), and Lemma B.21 gives a regular saturated $\Theta^+ \supseteq F^\perp$ with $m(\Theta^+) \ge m(F^\perp) - 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}} \ge \operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top) - 3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $v_{[i+1]} \in \overline{\Theta^+}$: the lattice for $i + 1$.

\emph{The short multiple.} Let $\Theta$ be the lattice for $N_0$, $B$ a basis matrix of it with a largest minor at $J$, and $z_0 \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ with $B z_0 = v_{[N_0]} \bmod q$, so $z_0 \ne 0 \bmod q$. The $z \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ congruent modulo $q$ to multiples of $z_0$ form a subgroup of index $q^{d-1}$, so the $B_J z$ form a lattice of determinant $h(\Theta)\, q^{d-1}$ in $\mathbb{R}^J$, and $d!\, h(\Theta)\, q^{d-1} \le \beta^d$ by (I6): $h(\Theta) \le H_1 \le \beta$, $2 h(\Theta)\, q \le 2 H_2\, q \le \beta^2$, or $6 h(\Theta)\, q^2 \le 6 \lfloor H_3 \rfloor q^2 \le \beta^3$, as heights are integers. By Minkowski's second theorem again, the successive minima of this lattice for $\|\cdot\|_1$ have $\lambda_1^d \le \lambda_1 \cdots \lambda_d \le d!\, h(\Theta)\, q^{d-1} \le \beta^d$, so it has a nonzero point $B_J z$ with $\|B_J z\|_1 = \lambda_1 \le \beta$. Then $x := B z$ is congruent modulo $q$ to a multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$, a nonzero one as $0 < \|x\|_\infty \le \|x_J\|_1 \le \beta < q$ (Lemma B.17(a), (I6)): $x$ is a short multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$, and extended by zeros it is one of $v$ with $x_0 = 0$.
add.explain: Under conditions (I1) to (I6) on (q, N, g, θ, β): every nonzero v in F_q^(N+1) with v_0 = 0 and gp(v^⊤) > θ has a short multiple, that is an integer vector x with ‖x‖_∞ ≤ β and x_0 = 0 whose reduction mod q is a nonzero multiple of v. Proof idea: Read the coordinates of v one at a time, keeping a saturated integer lattice of rank at most three whose reduction contains the prefix. Trimming, a lattice-point count that rules out wrap-around mod q, and a regularization step extend it; Minkowski's theorem in the last lattice gives the short multiple.

add.label: Lemma B.6'
add.name: A witness in the row space
add.statement: A nonzero usable stack whose row space has dimension at most three and contains no kernel vector has a witness of $S$ in its row space.
add.proof:
\emph{Step 1: one symmetric tensor.} Let $\mathbf{W}$ be such a stack, with row space $\mathcal{V}$. The symmetric matrices $W_U$ and $W_V$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ determine the stack, and with $z_s := \sigma^s(z)$ and $W_s := W_U$, $W_V$, and $\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ for $s \in I := \{n/2 - 1, n/2, n/2 + 1\}$, the ties are $W_s\, z_{s'} = W_{s'}\, z_s$ for $s, s' \in I$. Let $d := \dim \mathcal{V}$, let the columns of $\mathcal{U} \in \mathbb{F}_q^{(N+1) \times d}$ be a basis of $\mathcal{V}$, with rows $u_i \in \mathbb{F}_q^d$, which span $\mathbb{F}_q^d$, and let $h_s := \mathcal{U}^\top z_s = \sigma^s(h_0)$. The entries of $h_0$, the values of $z$ on the basis, are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_q$, as $\mathcal{V}$ contains no kernel vector; so $d \le n$, and by Lemma B.5 the $h_s$, $s \in I$, span $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^d$, as $d \le 3$. Each $W_s$ is symmetric with columns in the $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$-span of $\mathcal{V}$, so $W_s = \mathcal{U}\, \Xi_s\, \mathcal{U}^\top$ for a unique symmetric $\Xi_s$, and the ties read $\Xi_s\, h_{s'} = \Xi_{s'}\, h_s$. So if $\sum_{s \in I} \varrho_s h_s = 0$, then $(\sum_s \varrho_s \Xi_s)\, h_{s'} = \Xi_{s'} \sum_s \varrho_s h_s = 0$ for all $s'$, so $\sum_s \varrho_s \Xi_s = 0$, as the $h_{s'}$ span. Hence there is a linear map $\Xi$ from $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^d$ to symmetric matrices with $\Xi(h_s) = \Xi_s$ for $s \in I$, and the trilinear form $\Xi(h; u, u') := u^\top\, \Xi(h)\, u'$ is symmetric in $u$ and $u'$ and, by the ties, in $h$ and $u'$, hence in all three. Booleanity at $j \in [N]$ is linear over $\mathbb{F}_q$, so the $W_s$ satisfy it: $\Xi(h; u_j, u_j - u_0) = 0$ for $h = h_s$, hence for all $h$. Also $\Xi_s = \sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ for $s \in \{n/2-1, n/2\}$, as $\sigma^n = \mathrm{id}$ and $\sigma^{n/2}$ fixes $W_V$, a polynomial in $T^2$.

\emph{Step 2: cubes of Boolean points, for $u_0 \ne 0$.} Extend $l_0 := u_0$ by vectors $l_k := u_{j_k}$, $k \in [d-1]$, to a basis of $\mathbb{F}_q^d$. For $\delta \in \{0,1\}^{d-1}$ let $p_\delta \in \mathbb{F}_q^d$ be the point with $\langle l_0, p_\delta \rangle = 1$ and $\langle l_k, p_\delta \rangle = \delta_k$, and let $w_\delta := \mathcal{U} p_\delta \in \mathcal{V}$, an assignment, as its entry $0$ is $\langle u_0, p_\delta \rangle = 1$. By Booleanity at the $j_k$ and symmetry, $\Xi(l_a; l_b, l_c)$ depends only on the set $A \subseteq [d-1]$ of the nonzero indices among $a, b, c$, and the cube $\langle h, p_\delta \rangle \langle u, p_\delta \rangle \langle u', p_\delta \rangle$ of $p_\delta$ has the value $\delta^A := \prod_{k \in A} \delta_k$ there. The matrix $(\delta^A)_{A, \delta}$ is invertible, as the monomials $\delta^A$ are a basis of the functions on the Boolean cube. So there are $c_\delta \in \mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ with $\Xi(h) = \sum_{\delta} c_\delta\, \langle h, p_\delta \rangle\, p_\delta\, p_\delta^\top$; and the squares $p_\delta\, p_\delta^\top$ are linearly independent, as they have the values $\delta^A$ on the pairs $(l_a, l_b)$, whose sets $A$ are all the subsets of $[d-1]$, as $d - 1 \le 2$. Let $\bar z_\delta := z(w_\delta) = \langle h_0, p_\delta \rangle$, nonzero as $w_\delta$ is no kernel vector; then $\langle h_s, p_\delta \rangle = \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)$, so $\Xi_s = \sum_\delta c_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)\, p_\delta p_\delta^\top$. Comparing the coefficients of the squares, which are over $\mathbb{F}_q$, in $\Xi_s = \sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ gives $c_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta) = \sigma^s(c_\delta)\, \bar z_\delta$ for $s \in \{n/2-1, n/2\}$: so $\sigma^{n/2-1}$ and $\sigma^{n/2}$, hence $\sigma$, fix $c_\delta / \bar z_\delta$, and $c_\delta = \chi_\delta\, \bar z_\delta$ with $\chi_\delta \in \mathbb{F}_q$. So $W_s = \mathcal{U}\, \Xi_s\, \mathcal{U}^\top = \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \bar z_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)\, w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ for $s \in I$.

\emph{Step 3: a witness, for $u_0 \ne 0$.} Let $\varrho$ be a linear function of a matrix, with coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_q$, whose vanishing is one of the tests; as $\mathbf{W}$ passes, $\varrho$ vanishes on every $W_c$. As $\sigma^j(T) = \omega^j T$, each $W_s$ is a combination of the $W_c$ over $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$. So $\varrho$ vanishes on $W_s = \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \bar z_\delta\, \sigma^s(\bar z_\delta)\, w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ for $s \in I$; that is, $h_0^\top \mathcal{Q}\, h_s = 0$ for $\mathcal{Q} := \sum_\delta \chi_\delta\, \varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)\, p_\delta p_\delta^\top$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$. As the $h_s$ span, $h_0^\top \mathcal{Q} = 0$; so $\mathcal{Q} = 0$, as the entries of $h_0$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{F}_q$, and $\chi_\delta\, \varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top) = 0$, as the squares are linearly independent. As $\mathbf{W}$ is nonzero and $W_U$, $W_V$ determine it, some $W_s$ is nonzero, so some $\chi_\delta$ is nonzero. For this $\delta$, $\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top) = 0$ for every test: $w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ passes, so the assignment $w_\delta \in \mathcal{V}$ is a witness of $S$ (Definition 4.2).

\emph{Step 4: the case $u_0 = 0$ does not occur.} If $u_0 = 0$, we show $\Xi = 0$; then every $W_s$ is zero, so the stack is zero, contrary to the hypothesis. Booleanity reads $\Xi(h; u_j, u_j) = 0$, and some $u_j$ form a basis $l_1, \dots, l_d$ of $\mathbb{F}_q^d$; so by symmetry $\Xi(l_a; l_b, l_c) = 0$ unless $a$, $b$, $c$ are distinct. Hence $\Xi = 0$ if $d \le 2$. If $d = 3$, let $t := \Xi(l_1; l_2, l_3)$; then $\Xi(h; l_b, l_c)$ is $t$ times the coordinate of $h$ at $l_a$ for distinct $a$, $b$, $c$, so $\Xi_s = \sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ gives $t\, h_s = \sigma^s(t)\, h_0$ for $s \in \{n/2-1, n/2\}$, as $\sigma^s(h_{n-s}) = h_0$. So $t = 0$, as $h_{n/2-1}, h_{n/2}$ are not both multiples of $h_0$ (Lemma B.5).
add.explain: A nonzero usable stack of rank at most three without kernel vector has a witness in its row space.

add.label: Lemma B.9'
add.name: Lifting step
add.statement: Let $2\beta < q$ and $24\beta^4 < q^3$. There is a deterministic algorithm that returns, on input a nonzero $v \in \mathbb{F}_q^{N+1}$ with $v_0 = 0$, a short multiple of $v$, or $\bot$ if there is none. Its running time is polynomial in $N$ and $\log q$.
add.proof:
Drop the coordinate $0$, reorder the others, and scale $v$ so that $v_1 = 1$. For $i \in [N]$ let $\mathcal{L}_i \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^i$ be the lattice of the $x$ congruent modulo $q$ to $x_1 (v_1, \dots, v_i)$, and call a vector $x$ \emph{bounded} if $\|x\|_\infty \le \beta$. As $2\beta < q$, the short multiples of $v$ are the nonzero bounded vectors of $\mathcal{L}_N$. The bounded vectors of $\mathcal{L}_i$ span a space of dimension at most three: four of them are linearly dependent, as each of their $4 \times 4$ minors is divisible by $q^3$, because modulo $q$ they lie on a line, and is at most $4!\, \beta^4 < q^3$ in absolute value.

Starting from $\mathcal{M}_1 = \mathbb{Z}$, the algorithm computes for $i = 2, \dots, N$ a basis of a lattice $\mathcal{M}_i \subseteq \mathcal{L}_i$ of rank at most three containing the bounded vectors of $\mathcal{L}_i$, and returns a nonzero one of $\mathcal{L}_N$, or $\bot$ if there is none. The first $i$ entries of a bounded vector $y$ of $\mathcal{L}_{i+1}$ form a bounded vector of $\mathcal{L}_i$, in $\mathcal{M}_i$; so $y$ lies in the lattice $\mathcal{N}$ generated by $q\, e_{i+1}$ and the basis vectors $x$ of $\mathcal{M}_i$, each extended by an entry in $[0, q)$ congruent to $x_1 v_{i+1}$.

Written in the at most four coefficients of these generators, which lie in $\mathcal{L}_{i+1}$, these $y$ are the integer solutions of $2(i+1)$ linear inequalities, and one lies outside the span of those found exactly if one of the at most four functionals in a basis of the integer functionals vanishing on this span is at least $1$ or at most $-1$ on it. So a round of at most eight integer programs \cite[Section 1]{Len83} finds a further solution or shows that those found span all, in dimension $d \le 3$: at most four rounds. Let $\mathcal{M}_{i+1}$ consist of the vectors of $\mathcal{N}$ in this span, which include all these $y$; the algorithm keeps the basis of it whose projection to $d$ coordinates, on which the bounded vectors found have a nonzero minor $h$, is in Hermite normal form \cite[Section 2, Theorem 2]{KB79}. Its entries are at most $d \cdot d!\, \beta^d \le 18\beta^3$ in absolute value, as a $d \times d$ minor of bounded vectors is at most $d!\, \beta^d$: at these coordinates they are at most the projected lattice's determinant, which divides $h$, and by Cramer's rule the others are combinations of these $d$ whose coefficients are such minors divided by $h$. By Cramer's rule, a bounded vector has coefficients at most $24\beta \max\{18\beta^3, q\}^3$; so all numbers have $O(\log q)$ bits. Hermite normal forms also give the functionals and $\mathcal{M}_{i+1}$, and the cited algorithms are polynomial.
add.explain: If 2β < q and 24β⁴ < q³, a deterministic algorithm LIFT returns, for a nonzero v with v_0 = 0, a short multiple of v, or ⊥ if there is none, in time polynomial in N and log q. Proof idea: Add one coordinate at a time, keeping a lattice of rank at most three that contains all bounded vectors; each extension is a few integer programs and Hermite normal forms in dimension at most four.

add.label: Lemma B.12'
add.name: First marks
add.statement: Let $u := 2Q + 2$. The first mark of a run is (a) $\mathsf{init}$ with probability at most $\sum_{s \in \{1,2,T\}} \binom{L_s}{2}\, \varepsilon_f$; (b) $\mathsf{guess}$ with probability at most $2^{\lambda}/N_{\mathsf{free}}$; (c) charged with probability at most $N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u)\, (\theta + \varepsilon_f) + \bigl( \binom{L + 3u}{2} + L + 3u \bigr)\, \varepsilon_f$.
add.proof:
\emph{(a)} The mark $\mathsf{init}$ requires two received elements of one group with equal exponents and expressions that are not formally equal. For a fixed pair and every $r$ this has probability at most $\varepsilon_f$ over $\mathbf{c}$: in $\mathbb{G}_1$ or $\mathbb{G}_2$ by Lemma B.4(e), and for the pair $G_T$, $\mathsf{K}^\alpha$, with values $1$ and $\alpha\kappa$, by Lemma B.4(c); and $\mathbb{G}_s$ has $\binom{L_s}{2}$ pairs.

\emph{(b)} In $\mathsf{R}_\$$, sample $\mathsf{lab}_T$ lazily, deciding whether a string is a label, and of which element, only for the two received labels of $\mathbb{G}_T$ and, at each call, at most two operands and a result's label: at most $2 + 3Q$ strings, of which those that are labels have entries until the first mark. So $\mathsf{guess}$ is set at a query to $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ before which $[\kappa]_T$ has no label. At such a query, given the other randomness of $\mathsf{R}_\$$, which is independent of $\mathsf{lab}_T$, and the sampler's earlier decisions, which together determine the query, its label is uniform among the $U \ge 2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}} - 2 - 3Q \ge N_{\mathsf{free}}$ undecided strings, so it is the query's string with probability at most $1/U$. A union bound over the at most $Q_H \le 2^\lambda$ queries gives (b).

\emph{(c), Step 1: the two games agree until a collision.} Sample the label injections of $\mathsf{R}_\$$, independent of $h$ and $H_{\mathsf{key}}$, lazily, given their images, deciding a label's exponent when it gets an entry \cites[proof of Theorem 1]{EC:Shoup97}{EC:BonBoy04a}. With the evaluation first, this is the symbolic game with value equality in place of formal equality, except that $\mathsf{R}_\$$ redraws a new guess variable's value if an entry already has it, which is a collision. So on the same randomness, until a collision, both games make the same calls and queries with equal answers, the monitor's table in $\mathsf{R}_\$$ is that of the symbolic game, and in each group its entries have distinct values, their labels' exponents, and no other element has a label yet. The first collision's call is the same; its answer may differ.

\emph{Step 2: a charged first mark gives a bad event.} Let the first mark of $\mathsf{R}_\$$ be charged. No two received elements collide, as this sets $\mathsf{init}$, and by Step 1 the monitor sets no mark until a collision occurs at a call or $\mathcal{A}$ queries $H_{\mathsf{key}}$ at the target label. If a collision comes first, the first one is bad. Suppose that it is good, with later entry $\mathsf{X}$ and earlier entry $\mathsf{X}'$. As $\mathsf{X} - \mathsf{X}'$ lies in $\mathbb{G}_T$ and has no guess variable, $\mathsf{X}$ is not a new guess variable, which occurs in its difference with every earlier entry; so $\mathsf{X}$ is a result. In $\mathsf{R}_\$$ it has the value of $\mathsf{X}'$, hence the label of $\mathsf{X}'$, and the monitor sets $\mathsf{diff}(\mathsf{X}^\circ - \mathsf{X}'^\circ)$, a good first mark: a contradiction. If the query comes first, it sets the first mark, which is not $\mathsf{guess}$; so (M4) reads the entry of the target label, a key value by Step 1, and a bad one: the mark is $\mathsf{coll}$ if it has a guess variable, and else a $\mathsf{key}(\mathsf{D})$ that is not good.

\emph{Step 3: a bad event is unlikely.} Fix a symbolic game and in it two entries, or one entry; we bound the probability over the evaluation that they form a bad event.
\emph{(i) $\mathsf{D}$ has a guess variable: at most $\varepsilon_f$.} The coefficient in $\mathsf{D}$ of some product of guess variables is not formally zero: a constant, or an expression of $\mathbb{G}_1$ or $\mathbb{G}_2$ whose value at every $r$ is then zero with probability at most $\varepsilon_f < 1$ over $\mathbf{c}$ (Lemma B.4(e)). So for every $r$, $\varpi \cdot (\operatorname{val}(\mathsf{D}) - \chi\kappa)$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\mathbf{c}$ and the guess variables, of total degree at most $d_f + 1$ by Lemma B.3, as $\varpi$ has degree five, and by Schwartz's lemma it vanishes with probability at most $(d_f + 1)/(q - D) \le \varepsilon_f$.
\emph{(ii) $\mathsf{D}$ has none: at most $\theta + \varepsilon_f$.} Over $\mathbf{c}$, the bound is $\varepsilon_f$ in $\mathbb{G}_1$ or $\mathbb{G}_2$ (Lemma B.4(e)) and in $\mathbb{G}_T$ at an $r$ at which $\mathsf{D}$ is not $\chi\kappa$ identically (Lemma B.4(c)). Every other $r$ satisfies $W_c\, r = u_c$ for the mark stack $\mathbf{W}$ of $\mathsf{D}$ and its vectors $u_c$ (Lemma B.4(a)); if there is one, $\mathbf{W}$ is nonzero, as $\mathsf{D}$ is not $\chi\kappa$ formally (Lemma B.4(b), (d)), and light, as the event is bad, so these $r$ have probability at most $\operatorname{gp}(\mathbf{W}) \le \theta$.

\emph{Step 4: counts.} A call adds at most three entries, two guessed operands and a result; of the at most $L + 3Q$ entries, at most $3Q$ have a guess variable, and case (i) covers at most $\binom{L + 3Q}{2}$ pairs and $3Q \le L + 3u$ key values, as $u = 2Q + 2$. In case (ii) a collision at call $j$ pairs its result, as $\mathsf{D}$ has no guess variable (Step 2), with one of at most $L + 3j - 1$ other entries, and a key value is a result or one of the two received elements of $\mathbb{G}_T$: at most $\sum_{j=1}^{Q} (L + 3j - 1) + Q + 2 \le N_{\mathrm{cmp}}(u)$ events. A union bound gives the claim.
add.explain: The first mark is charged (a collision with a guessed label, or a comparison that is not a good mark) with probability at most N_(cmp)(u)(θ + ε_f) + (C(L+3u, 2) + L + 3u)·ε_f. Proof idea: Shoup's simulation argument: a symbolic game answers by formal equality and agrees with the real run until two values collide. A bad collision has probability at most ε_f over the coins, or at most θ over the search vector when its stack is light. Union bound over the comparisons.

discharge.argument: The second sentence of Lemma B.2' is the demand: its two premises are admissibility condition (P5) word for word, and its conclusion is E(2Q+2) <= (Q+1)/2^lambda for every integer 0 <= Q < 2^lambda.
Lemma 5.5' states |r(w) - c_w| <= B for every r in the support of D_g, the sampler of Enc in Appendix A, with c_w the center used by Dec; this is the demanded bound word for word.

Proposition 5.7 is stated for Praxis as specified in Appendix A, whose Enc draws r from the centered sampler D_g and whose Dec uses the center c_w for D_g. For exactly this r and c_w, Lemma 5.5' states the bound E[(r(w) - c_w)^2] <= (g sqrt((N+4)/48) + 3/2)^2 with the same constants as the second case of the base lemma. Jensen's inequality then gives E sqrt|r(w) - c_w| <= (g sqrt((N+4)/48) + 3/2)^(1/2) = O(sqrt(g) N^(1/4)), the expected search of the demand. The dropped case (independent entries, Section 5.1) is not the scheme of Appendix A.

(a) A good mark's stack W is heavy (App. B.4), that is, gp(W) > θ (Definition 4.4). Lemma 4.5'(a) states gp(W) ≤ g^(−rank W) for every stack. If rank W ≥ 4 then gp(W) ≤ g^(−4), as g ≥ 1, and g^(−4) < θ is one of the conditions (P3) of admissible parameters (Sec. 5.4); so W would be light. Hence rank W ≤ 3. (b) The kernel vector v found lies in the row space of the heavy mark stack W, so Lemma 4.5'(b) gives gp(v^⊤) ≥ gp(W) > θ. A kernel vector is nonzero with z(v) = 0 (App. B.3), and z(v) = 0 means φ_e(v) = 0 for every e, with φ_0(v) = v_0 (Definition 5.1); so v_0 = 0. (P3) is the conditions (I1) to (I6) of Lemma B.7', whose statement then gives a short multiple of v. (c) Lemma B.8' states, under (P3), that for a short multiple x of a kernel vector, x̂ solves MSIS for the columns 1, …, ℓ of M, with 0 < ‖x̂‖_∞ ≤ β and A·x̂ = 0 mod q: this is clause (c) of Lemma B.8' word for word.

A good mark's stack W is heavy (App. B.4), that is, gp(W) > θ (Definition 4.4). Lemma 4.5'(a) states gp(W) ≤ g^(−rank W) for every stack. If rank W ≥ 4 then gp(W) ≤ g^(−4), as g ≥ 1, and g^(−4) < θ is one of the conditions (P3) of admissible parameters (Sec. 5.4); so W would be light. Hence rank W ≤ 3.

The statement is the demand: the rank of a stack is by definition the dimension of its row space (Definition 4.4), so the hypotheses (nonzero, usable, rank at most three, no kernel vector in the row space) and the conclusion (a witness of S in the row space) are the same.

The statement gives the algorithm LIFT that on a nonzero v with v_0 = 0 returns a short multiple of v, or bot if there is none: a short multiple whenever one exists, and nothing else. Same hypotheses.
The last sentence of the statement: the running time T_LIFT is polynomial in N and log q, same hypotheses.
